prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current state-of-the-art approaches for generating listening head animations leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict non-verbal responses based on speaker speech. However, these methods suffer from two critical limitations. First, they predominantly rely on a unimodal input—textual speech content—thereby ignoring the rich acoustic and emotional context (prosody, timbre, facial affect) that fundamentally drives human conversational dynamics. Second, existing architectures entangle the generation of motion with the listener's identity. The model simultaneously learns "how to move" and "who is moving," resulting in poor generalization; changing the avatar's identity typically requires retraining the entire model.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that naturally occurring listener responses are a function of multimodal cues—specifically the interplay between semantic content, acoustic delivery, and the speaker's emotional state. By modeling these modalities jointly as a discrete sequence generation task, an LLM can infer more contextually appropriate reactions. Furthermore, we posit that listener identity and listener motion can be structurally disentangled. We propose that identity functions as a static "style" applied to dynamic "motion content," allowing us to generate high-fidelity, identity-agnostic motion codes that can be rendered onto any target face.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a two-stage framework: a **Multimodal-LM** for motion planning and an **Identity-Disentangled VQ-VAE** for motion rendering.

### 1. Multimodal Tokenization and Sequence Modeling
We aim to move beyond simple text-to-motion generation by treating the conversation as a multimodal stream. We will tokenize the input space into three distinct discrete representations:
*   **Speech Content:** Derived from Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to capture semantic meaning.
*   **Speech Acoustics:** Extracted via a neural audio codec to capture prosody, stress, and delivery style.
*   **Speaker Emotion:** Obtained by discretizing facial motion into categorical emotional states.

We will employ a Transformer-based LLM as the core generator. The model will ingest an interleaved sequence of these speaker tokens and autoregressively predict discrete **Listener Response tokens**. This allows the model to leverage the causal relationship between the speaker’s multimodal expression and the listener’s reaction.

### 2. Identity-Disentangled Motion Synthesis (VQ-VAE)
To solve the identity entanglement problem, we will design a specialized Vector Quantized-Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) that acts as the interface between the LLM's discrete output and the continuous 3D facial animation parameters.

*   **Identity Erasure (Encoder):** We will utilize **Instance Normalization** within the encoder. The intuition is to normalize the feature statistics of the input motion, effectively stripping away the static "identity" attributes (individual facial structure) while preserving the dynamic "motion" content. This forces the codebook to learn generic, identity-agnostic motion primitives.
*   **Identity Injection (Decoder):** We will employ **Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN)** in the decoder. During the reconstruction (or generation) phase, we will inject a target identity embedding to modulate the normalized features. This allows the decoder to "paint" the generic motion codes with the specific structural and stylistic characteristics of any desired avatar.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Advancement:** A novel formulation of listening head generation that integrates acoustics and visual emotion alongside semantics, providing a more holistic model of dyadic communication.
*   **Architectural Novelty:** A strategy for disentangling static identity from dynamic motion in facial animation using normalization techniques within a VQ-VAE framework.
*   **Practical Utility:** The ability to control listener identity flexibly without retraining, enabling a single generative model to drive diverse digital avatars with high fidelity.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

### Datasets and Processing
*   **Datasets:** We utilized two listener datasets: L2L-trevor (single-listener, featuring Trevor Noah) and RealTalk (multi-listener).
*   **Preprocessing:** 
    *   Raw videos were segmented into 8-second segments.
    *   Speech separation was performed to identify listener segments.
    *   EMOCA was used to extract 3DMM parameters for both speaker and listener and to recognize speaker emotions.
    *   Whisper was used for text transcription.
    *   SpeechTokenizer was used to extract acoustic information.
*   **Data Splits:**
    *   **L2L-trevor:** 2,366 training segments, 222 validation segments, 543 test segments.
    *   **RealTalk:** 2,714 training segments, 238 validation segments, 808 test segments.

### Evaluation Metrics
We evaluated performance based on realism, diversity, and synchrony:
*   **Realism:** L2 Distance (L2) and Frechet Distance (FD).
*   **Diversity:** Variation and Diversity scores.
*   **Synchrony:** Paired Frechet Distance (P-FD) and L2 Affect (measuring facial affect accuracy).

### Baselines Compared
*   **GT:** Ground Truth.
*   **Random:** Random listener sequence from the training set.
*   **NN Facial Motion:** Nearest neighbor in training set based on cosine similarity of facial motion.
*   **NN Speech Content:** Nearest neighbor in training set based on text embeddings (Sentence-BERT).
*   **Naive Random Walk:** Random walk over codebook indices using a naive VQ-VAE without identity disentanglement.
*   **LM-listener:** Previous state-of-the-art method using a naive VQ-VAE and unimodal speech content inputs.
    *   Evaluated with GPT2-Medium backbone.
    *   Evaluated with LLAMA2-7B backbone.

### Implementation Details
*   **VQ-VAE Settings:**
    *   Codebook size ($V_{LR}$): 256.
    *   Codebook embedding dimension ($d_c$): 512.
    *   Downsampling rate ($r$): 8.
    *   Loss weights: $\mathcal{L}_{commit} = 0.02$, $\mathcal{L}_{veloc} = 0.5$, others set to 1.
*   **Language Model Settings:**
    *   Models: GPT2-Medium (full parameter fine-tuning) and LLAMA2-7B (LoRA fine-tuning).
    *   Optimizer: AdamW.
    *   Sampling: Greedy sampling used during testing for motion tokens.
*   **Normalization Strategy:** We tested Instance Normalization (IN) in the encoder and Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN) in the decoder for identity disentanglement.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

### Performance Analysis (Textual & Graphic)
*   **General Performance:** On the L2L-trevor dataset, our method improved L2 and FD metrics by 38% and 45% respectively compared to the previous state-of-the-art. On the RealTalk dataset, the improvements were 60% in L2 and 65% in FD.
*   **Codebook Sampling:** Our "Random Walk" method (using the identity-disentangled codebook) significantly outperformed the "Naive Random Walk" and even surpassed the LM-listener baseline, indicating that the identity VQ-VAE learned robust, individualized motion priors.
*   **Ablation Findings (Modality):** Using implicit speech content (iSC) yielded no gains over text (W). Adding Speech Acoustics (SA) alone to text showed limited improvement. However, adding Emotion (emo) significantly improved L2 Affect. The combination of W + SA + emo yielded the best results across all metrics.
*   **Ablation Findings (Normalization):** Normalization layers improved reconstruction by handling input variance better than dataset-wide statistics. Adaptive normalization in the decoder significantly improved the Commitment loss (Commit.), allowing the model to adjust output sequences based on identity.

### Visual Consistency and Context (Figure 4 Analysis)
*   **Scenario 1 & 2 (Sarcasm/Humor):** The speaker used sarcastic humor (e.g., describing symptoms negatively but with a humorous style; stating "nobody wants to have dinner with me"). While the text was negative, the speaker's facial emotion was happy/humorous. Our model successfully generated synchronized laughter/smiling, whereas the baseline failed to capture the humorous context from text alone.
*   **Scenario 3 & 4 (Serious Tone):** The speaker used positive words ("best", "love") but maintained a serious/sad facial expression and tone. Our model generated calm/serious listener expressions, aligning with the actual emotional state rather than the positive text semantics. The baseline generated positive expressions (smiles) based solely on the positive words.

### Identity Disentanglement (Figure 5 Analysis)
*   **Naive VQ-VAE:** Produced fixed expressions and poses for specific motion tokens regardless of the target identity. It failed to capture individual style nuances.
*   **Identity-Disentangled VQ-VAE (Ours):** Successfully adapted the same latent token to generate identity-specific expressions and poses. For example, for a "smile" token, it generated different smile styles (open-mouth vs. closed-mouth) appropriate to the specific listener identity.

### User Study Results
*   **Participants:** 33 volunteers.
*   **Comparison vs. LM-listener:** Volunteers preferred our method in 86.4% of instances based on emotional alignment and synchronization.
*   **Comparison vs. Ground Truth:** Volunteers preferred our method 65.8% of the time when compared to synthesized ground truth, indicating high perceptual realism.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

```latex
  \end{subfigure}

  \label{fig:short}

```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current state-of-the-art approaches for listening head generation, specifically those leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs), suffer from two critical technical deficiencies. First, they rely on a unimodal approach that processes solely the semantic content of the speaker's speech. This ignores vital non-verbal cues—such as acoustic prosody and speaker emotion—that govern the dynamics of dyadic conversation. Second, existing architectures entangle listener identity with response generation. The decoder is typically tasked with learning both the static identity geometry and the dynamic motion simultaneously. This entanglement compromises output fidelity and precludes generalization; changing the listener's identity currently requires retraining the entire model, which is computationally inefficient and limits scalability.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the semantic reasoning capabilities of LLMs can be extended to non-verbal communication by tokenizing multimodal signals (acoustics and emotion) alongside text. Furthermore, we hypothesize that listener identity can be rigorously treated as a "style" attribute and disentangled from "content" (motion) within a VQ-VAE framework. By applying Instance Normalization (IN) to erase identity in the encoder and Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN) to inject identity in the decoder, we will achieve high-fidelity, identity-agnostic motion generation that allows for flexible identity control without retraining.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework comprising two primary modules: a Multimodal-LM for generating listener motion tokens and an Identity-Disentangled VQ-VAE for synthesizing photorealistic video from those tokens.

### 1. Notation and Preliminaries
We define the input speaker video of $T$ frames as $t = \{ 1, \dots, T \}$. The corresponding facial motion is $\mathbf{F}^s = \{ f_1^s, \dots, f_T^s \}$ and audio is $\mathbf{A}^s$. We define $f_t^s = [\psi_t^s, \theta_t^s]$, comprising 3DMM facial expression parameters $\psi$ and head pose parameters $\theta$. We will explicitly exclude the shape parameter $\beta$ from $f$ to facilitate disentanglement. The target output is the listener facial motion $\mathbf{F}^l$.

### 2. Multimodal Speaker Input Processing
We will decouple the speaker's input into three discrete token streams:

1.  **Speech Content ($\mathbf{W}$):** We will use a pretrained ASR model (Whisper) to transcribe $\mathbf{A}^s$ into text tokens $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$, where $N$ is the token count.
2.  **Speech Acoustics ($\mathbf{SA}$):** To capture prosody and timbre, we will utilize a pretrained SpeechTokenizer (a Residual Vector Quantization network). We will extract the output of the second quantizer from the 8 available quantizers to balance information density. This yields acoustic tokens $\mathbf{SA} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 1}$.
3.  **Speaker Emotion ($\mathbf{emo}$):** We will downsample speaker motion $\mathbf{F}^s$ by a rate $r$. For each group, we will use the EMOCA emotion recognition module to predict a probability distribution over emotional states. We will select the state with the highest probability as the discrete emotion token, resulting in $\mathbf{emo} \in \mathbb{R}^{(T/r) \times 1}$.

### 3. Multimodal-LM Architecture
We will adapt a transformer-based LLM, denoted as $\mathcal{G}$. We will initialize a new embedding matrix $E_{\mathrm{MM}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(\bar{V}_{\mathrm{LR}} + V_{\mathrm{SA}} + V_{\mathrm{emo}}) \times \bar{d}_w}$ to handle the new modalities, where $V$ represents the vocabulary size of listener responses, acoustics, and emotions respectively. An affine projection layer will be appended to the output to predict listener tokens.

**Sequential Organization:**
We will construct the input sequence $\mathcal{S}$ in an interleaved format to preserve causality:
$$ \mathcal{S} = \{ \mathbf{W}^h, \mathbf{W}_{1:r}, \mathbf{SA}_{1:r}, \mathbf{emo}_1, \mathbf{LR}_1, \mathbf{W}_{r+1:2r}, \mathbf{SA}_{r+1:2r}, \dots, \mathbf{LR}_{T/r} \} $$
where $\mathbf{W}^h$ represents historical context tokens and $\mathbf{LR}$ are the listener response tokens we aim to generate.

**Training Strategy:**
We will train $\mathcal{G}$ in two stages:
1.  **Speaker Understanding Pretraining:** We optimize the model to predict acoustic and emotion tokens based on speech content. The loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pre}}$ is defined as:
    $$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pre}} = - \sum_{j=1}^{N+M+T/r} \log \operatorname*{Pr} [\mathcal{G}(S^{\prime}_{1:N^{\prime}+j-1}) = S^{\prime}_{N^{\prime}+j}] $$
    where $S'$ is a speaker-only sequence excluding listener tokens.
2.  **Listener Response Fine-tuning:** We optimize the model to predict the listener response tokens $\mathbf{LR}$. The loss $\mathcal{L}$ is defined as:
    $$ \mathcal{L} = - \sum_{i=1}^{T/r} \log \mathrm{Pr} [\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{W}^h, \mathbf{W}_{1:ri}, \mathbf{SA}_{1:ri}, \mathbf{emo}_{1:i-1}, \mathbf{LR}_{1:i-1}) = \mathbf{LR}_i] $$

### 4. Identity-Disentangled VQ-VAE
To map the predicted $\mathbf{LR}$ tokens to high-fidelity motion while controlling identity, we will construct a specialized VQ-VAE.

**Architecture:**
*   **Encoder:** Maps listener motion $\mathbf{F}^l$ to latent features $\mathbf{Z} = \{ z_1, \dots, z_{T/r} \}$. Crucially, we will employ **Instance Normalization (IN)** layers here to eliminate identity-specific variation (mean and variance) from the features.
*   **Quantizer:** We define a codebook $\mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d_c}$. We utilize a nearest-neighbor quantization function $Q$:
    $$ \mathbf{LR}_j = Q(z_i) = \arg \operatorname*{min}_{1 \leq j \leq K} \| z_i - \mathbf{LR}_j \|^2 $$
*   **Decoder:** Reconstructs motion from quantized latents $\mathbf{Z}_Q$. To re-inject identity, we will use **Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN)**. The decoder will take the listener's 3DMM identity parameter $\beta^l$ as a conditional input to modulate the feature maps:
    $$ \hat{\mathbf{F}}^l = \text{Decoder}(\mathbf{Z}_Q, \beta^l) $$

**Training Objectives:**
The VQ-VAE will be trained using a composite loss function including reconstruction loss ($\mathcal{L}_{rec}$), commitment loss ($\mathcal{L}_{commit}$), and velocity loss ($\mathcal{L}_{veloc}$).

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Multimodal Integration:** We expect to demonstrate that integrating discrete acoustic and emotional tokens into the LLM context window significantly enhances the contextual appropriateness and affect alignment of generated listener responses compared to text-only baselines.
2.  **Identity Disentanglement:** We will provide a theoretical framework for separating static identity from dynamic motion in listening head generation. By utilizing IN/AdaIN within the VQ-VAE, we expect to achieve high-fidelity results that allow for zero-shot identity transfer without model retraining.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.

notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
